Muszyna Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Muszyna, Poland

Not demolished. Muszyna, first mentioned in the 13th century and granted town rights around 1340, was owned by the Bishops of Kraków from the late 14th century until 1781 under the so-called 'State of Muszyna.' Jewish settlement, initially prohibited, developed from the mid-19th century after Austrian-partition restrictions lifted; the community, originally subordinate to Nowy Sącz's kehilla, gained independence by century's end, growing to 748 residents (23%) by 1939. In late 1940, Germans displaced all Jews from area health resort towns (including Muszyna, Grybów, and Bobowa) to the Nowy Sącz Ghetto, liquidated in 1942 with deportations to Bełżec and Auschwitz. This cemetery, likely founded toward the end of the 19th century on a steep slope, was largely stripped of tombstones after the war; cleanup only began in 1995, with fencing funded by the Nissenbaum Family Foundation in 2016.
